subject: ss-medical-oncology
title: Opioid receptors, ceiling effect, fentanyl patch and rescue dosing

steps.tx: Opioid-induced **respiratory depression** is the most serious side effect of these drugs. Most opioid analgesics act at the **mu opioid receptor**. Activating mu receptors in the brainstem breathing centers slows and shallows each breath, and the effect depends on the dose. Sedation usually appears first and gives an early warning. A breathing rate below 10 breaths per minute is a danger sign.

nodes.label: Slow, shallow breathing; rate falls below 10 per minute

steps.tx: **Naloxone** is a **pure antagonist** at the mu receptor, so it reverses opioid effects, including depressed breathing. In an unstable patient, clinicians give it intravenously in **titrated** doses. They dilute 0.4 milligrams (mg) in 10 milliliters (mL) of saline. Then they give 1 to 2 mL every 30 to 60 seconds until breathing improves.

steps.tx: **Full agonists** such as morphine, fentanyl, oxycodone, hydromorphone and methadone have **no ceiling effect** on pain relief. The right dose is therefore the one that controls the pain. The **partial agonist** buprenorphine behaves differently, with a **ceiling effect** on analgesia. Beyond a certain dose, extra buprenorphine adds no pain relief.

steps.tx: **Mixed agonist-antagonists** such as butorphanol can cause **withdrawal** in a patient who is already physically dependent on a pure opioid. Pentazocine, butorphanol and nalbuphine also reach an **analgesic ceiling**, so extra drug above a plateau dose adds little pain relief. Nalbuphine is also used for persistent itching caused by opioids.

steps.tx: A **transdermal fentanyl patch** is typically replaced every **72 hours**, and it delivers steady drug levels. Pain relief starts late, with an **onset delay** of about 12 to 15 hours after placement. Levels then need a further 24 to 72 hours to reach steady state. A **short-acting rescue** opioid covers that gap, and dose changes should not be made sooner than every 72 hours.

steps.tx: Fentanyl suits patients who cannot take oral medicines. Some studies show that it causes **less constipation** than oral morphine. The liver clears it without **active metabolites**, so it is a promising option when **renal insufficiency** (reduced kidney function) is present. Patients with **cachexia** (severe wasting) have little **adipose tissue** (body fat), so absorption from the patch may fall short.

steps.tx: **Breakthrough pain** is severe acute pain on top of chronic pain that is otherwise controlled. It needs a short-acting **rescue dose**. On a fixed schedule, the rescue dose is typically **5 to 15 percent** of the total 24-hour opioid requirement. For a patient on 300 milligrams of oral morphine a day, that means roughly 15 to 45 milligrams per rescue dose.

steps.tx: A **fentanyl patch** is meant only for **opioid-tolerant** patients with **chronic pain**. Heat over the patch, from a fever or a heating pad, speeds absorption and can cause **respiratory depression**. Dose increases should wait for steady state, which usually takes 3 to 6 days with a patch. Keep a rescue opioid ready during the early gap.
